items.title: The Place Called Dagon
items.author: Herbert Gorman
items.content:
Daniel Dreeme is a doctor who maintains a practice in the small and secluded community of Marlborough, Massachusetts. But his idyllic life takes a turn towards darkness when discovers that the town is home to an ancient cult who worships Satan as their true god.

A work of the “folk horror” genre, derives its plot from the pseudo-historical “witch-cult hypothesis,” which posits that witchcraft was practiced in secret in the Early Modern period. The book was likely an inspiration for some of H. P. Lovecraft’s later fiction, especially “The Shadow Over Innsmouth,” which shares the overall geographical location and many plot points.

items.title: Hand and Ring
items.author: Anna Katharine Green
items.content:
A conversation on the steps of a quiet courthouse in Sibley, New York turns to a chilling topic: how to commit the perfect murder. A mysterious stranger declares that the secret lies in striking a blow in a busy thoroughfare using a weapon found on the spot, allowing the tracks of innocent passersby to naturally erase those of the killer.

Then, minutes later and just yards away from where the conversation took place, a deaf widow is found brutally struck down in her dining room in the exact fashion the stranger had just described. The dying woman’s last words, “Hand! Ring! Ring! Hand!”, only confuse and misdirect the young detectives until Detective Gryce arrives.

This is the fourth novel to feature Detective Gryce, though in this one, Gryce doesn’t come into the picture until the end, where he plays a critical role in uncovering the true perpetrator.

items.title: The Lost Stradivarius
items.author: John Meade Falkner
items.content:
John Meade Falkner published his first novel, , in 1896. Set in the aristocratic milieu similar to the one Falkner grew up in, the story at first closely mirrors his own—that of a young man studying at Oxford—before taking a turn for the uncanny. From there it delves progressively deeper into old blasphemy and new madness.

proved to be the debut of a solid figure in the turn-of-the-century British literary milieu, influencing figures like M. R. James and Dorothy L. Sayers.

items.title: Racundra’s First Cruise
items.author: Arthur Ransome
items.content:
Arthur Ransome was working as a journalist in Russia during the First World War when he got the idea to build a sailboat. He asked his friend, a boat designer, to design one, and in 1922 it was finally completed in Estonia. But Ransome didn’t have enough time to sail it to England before winter, so instead he enlisted two unnamed companions, the Cook and the Ancient Mariner, to join him for maiden voyage across the Baltic Sea, from Riga to Helsinki and back.

is Ransome’s travelogue of this six week trip. Between both pleasant faring and treacherous weather, he and his tiny crew engage in various cozy episodes across the coasts and ports of Estonia, taking in the local color, haggling with the officials, and getting to know their new sailboat, all in a spirit of gentle adventure.

Though unnamed, the Cook is actually Leon Trotsky’s ex-private secretary, Ransome’s lover and later wife Evgenia Petrovna Shelepina, and the Ancient Mariner is Captain Carl Sehmel, who is also featured as a character in Ransome’s Swallows and Amazons series, in and .

items.title: The Man from the Clouds
items.author: J. Storer Clouston
items.content:
Roger Merton, a young naval lieutenant from the volunteer reserves, is on a balloon reconnaissance mission with an officer when their balloon loses its moorings and drifts into the fog. Blown to they know not where, Merton’s colleague bails, while Merton waits until he’s more certain of being over land.

When he does parachute to safety, Merton finds that he’s not in enemy territory, but rather in one of the islands in the North Sea off the Scottish coast. Still uncertain as to who inhabits it, he begins to suspect there may be treachery afoot. But where could German spies be hiding on such a barren island?

items.title: The Chink in the Armour
items.author: Marie Belloc Lowndes
items.content:
Sylvia Bailey, a beautiful young widow, and her friend Anna visit a fortune teller in Paris and receive ominous warnings: for Anna, that she’ll have an incredible streak of fortune at gambling but shortly lose her life, and for Sylvia that she’ll meet a great lover but somehow be strangled by her beloved pearl necklace, a piece of exceedingly great value purchased against her lawyer’s advice with much of the wealth her late husband bequeathed her. The fortune teller implores them not to leave Paris soon, and certainly not together, but, ignoring the advice, they make their way to the picturesque town of Lacville. There, they set about playing baccarat and making friends with the local characters—until a mysterious disappearance raises uneasy questions.

This hair-raising mystery is the first of Marie Belloc Lowndes’s novels to have been adapted to the screen, and it showcases her understanding of the inner life of women, the mindset of the gambler, and the discomforting experience of a silent haunting.

items.title: The Slaves of the Padishah
items.author: Mór Jókai
items.content:
Michael Teleki, a Transylvanian noble and councilor to Prince Apafi, is an ambitious and cunning politician who seeks to increase his power and social status. In order to do that, he attempts to manipulate members of the Ottoman Sultanate to attack Hungary, with hopes that he will become its Palatine.

A sequel to , The Slaves of the Padishah sees the return of most of the characters of the previous novel. Much like the first installment, this novel is a fictionalized version of real events: in this case, the loss of Turkish control over Hungary and the expansion of the Holy Roman Empire to territories previously controlled by the Sultanate.

items.title: A Treatise of Human Nature
items.author: David Hume
items.content:
In the , written in 1739, David Hume lays out his initial vision of our knowledge and understanding of the world, of the nature of our psychology and motivation, and, building on these, of moral and political philosophy.

In Book I, Hume considers our understanding of the world. With a keen critical perspective that is ever skeptical about abstract metaphysical claims, he follows other empiricists (such as Locke) in grounding our understanding in experience as the source of all our ideas and of their relations to each other. In one important line of argument, he raises what has come to be known as his “problem of induction” at the heart of our understanding of causation and of science, arguing that we have no reason to think that the future will be like the past, since our only evidence for that claim could be past experience—a problem that has plagued philosophers ever since.

In Book II, Hume turns from belief and reason to desire and the passions, famously arguing that “it is not contrary to reason to prefer the destruction of the whole world to the scratching of my finger”—that questions of what we to desire or value are not questions we can settle by appealing to beliefs and arguments. Rather, our desires and passions can be independent of our beliefs, so that values aren’t a the world, but are by us the world.

In Book III, Hume spells out the implications this view has for morality, and so for moral values and moral taste. In doing so, he emphasizes our sympathy for others and the need for us to use that sympathy so as to adopt “steady and general points of view” as the proper vantage point for engaging in moral criticism.

The was poorly received, with Hume himself writing that it fell “deadborn from the press.” He thought it an immature work, written as it was before he was 25 years old, and he later reworked his account from Book I in his Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding and from Book III in his Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals. Nonetheless, much of Hume’s dissatisfaction seems to be stylistic rather than substantive; philosophical scholarship has tended to focus on the over his other works, and it has remained highly influential to this day, shaping important strands of thought in philosophy and psychology.

items.title: If I Had a Father
items.author: George MacDonald
items.content: Attempting to earn the love of his estranged son Arthur, Col. Gervaise has been hired as his manservant. Unaware of the Colonel’s true identity, Arthur, a reclusive and brooding artist, longs to be left alone to sculpt his latest work: a Psyche, which he keeps hidden from any visitors. When an unruly and desperate Scotsman comes to Arthur’s studio in search of his own estranged child, Mattie, Col. Gervaise is given an opportunity to not only reunite Arthur with his father, but Mattie with hers as well.

items.title: The Birds
items.author: Aristophanes
items.content:
Two Athenians, lead by a crow and a jay sold to them as guides, have walked a long way away from their homeland because they’re fed up with its constant lawsuits. Finding the noble Epops, a talking hoopoe bird, they hatch a plan to join the birds in building a new city in the clouds where society will be better. The city, though, floating as it does in the sky, stops the smoke of the burnt sacrifices on the ground from reaching the gods in the heavens, and incurs their wrath.

, written in 414 BC, has most of Aristophanes’ common tropes: satire of the famous figures of Athens, puns and wordplay, and an unbelievable scenario. It’s regularly performed to this day, but its biggest impact in modern times is probably its contribution to the English language of the phrase “cloud cuckoo land,” a direct translation of the name the birds give their floating city.

This edition of is based on the unattributed translation and numerous annotations first published by The Athenian Society in 1912.

items.title: Krakatit
items.author: Karel Čapek
items.content:
An engineer named Prokop discovers a terrifying new explosive: one that releases the energy stored in matter itself. Though dazed by his discovery, Prokop immediately sees the dangers that this explosive will bring; but as others become aware of his discovery, they instead see a rare opportunity.

Part science fiction, part romance, and part satire, Prokop’s ensuing adventures are full of symbolism and surreal dreamlike encounters. Through Prokop, Čapek explores the relation of science to truth, and the moral responsibilities of scientists.

Though it was written in the 1920s, the explosive described in Krakatit can easily be reimagined as the atomic bomb. Shorty after World War II a Czech film adaptation was released which captured the anxiety created by such a real life weapon of mass destruction.

items.title: The Third Round
items.author: H. C. McNeile
items.content: Professor Goodman, an eccentric chemist, has made the breakthrough of a lifetime: he’s discovered a way to inexpensively manufacture flawless diamonds in the laboratory. To Goodman, the discovery is something that should be shared with the scientific community and the world at large; but to the heads of England’s diamond cartel, the discovery means the ruin of their business and the loss of their fortunes. In panic, they hire master criminal Carl Peterson to make sure the world never learns about Professor Goodman’s formula. Peterson, of course, wants the formula for his own diabolical reasons. There’s only one man who can save the Professor and keep his formula from falling into the wrong hands—gentleman adventurer Bulldog Drummond.

items.title: Short Fiction
items.author: Edgar Saltus
items.content:
Edgar Saltus was a writer of decadent fiction with a pessimistic bent and characterized by a wit reminiscent of Oscar Wilde. After his 1887 debut with he wrote many novels, novellas, and short stories in rapid succession, and to great success. Critics condemned his works as immoral and the public was scandalized, but for a while, Edgar Saltus was infamous. His stories weave a common thread: love, lust, greed, distrust, and deceit among the upper classes of late nineteenth-century New York, who also regularly retreat to Paris, the Riviera, London, and other destinations frequented by the era’s super-rich.

There are outliers. “A Transient Guest” finds its protagonist in the Dutch East-Indies. “Mary Magdalen,” an historical novella, recounts the final days of Jesus Christ through the perspective of the title character. And although “Madam Sapphira” is more in line with his other works, its story bears striking similarities to the circumstances surrounding Saltus’s highly publicized divorce from his first wife. Written to clear his name and that of his corespondents, its publication had the opposite effect.

After 1895, the name Edgar Saltus began to lose its luster. He continued to write and publish, but less often and to much less attention. At the same time, the cynical worldview that defined his early output shifted. Inspired by religious movement of Theosophy, he gradually became milder and more optimistic, the effect of which is noticeable in his later work.

During this second half of his career Saltus frequently reused and recycled ideas, phrases, passages, and even whole plots. This collection has been carefully edited to avoid including such obviously redundant material and to avoid overlap between these stories and other Standard Ebooks titles.

items.title: Poetry
items.author: John Donne
items.content:
John Donne composed poetry over the span of several decades, from the 1590s through the early years of the seventeenth century, during a period of profound religious, political, and cultural change in England. Unlike many of his contemporaries, Donne didn’t publish any collections of poetry during his lifetime. Instead, his poems circulated privately in handwritten manuscripts among friends, patrons, and members of the educated elite, acquiring a wide readership long before they appeared in print. The first collected edition was published posthumously in 1633, two years after Donne’s death, and was followed by numerous expanded editions that included additional poems discovered in manuscript. This collection brings together all of Donne’s diverse body of work, from his youthful satires, elegies, and love lyrics, to his later religious verses and Holy Sonnets, illustrating the remarkable range and enduring influence of one of the greatest poets of the English Renaissance.

John Donne’s most popular poems include “The Flea,” “A Valediction Forbidding Mourning,” “The Sun Rising,” “The Canonization,” and “Holy Sonnet XIV.”

items.title: Revolving Lights
items.author: Dorothy M. Richardson
items.content:
Series protagonist Miriam Henderson puts an end to her relationship with co-lodger Michael Shatov, a young Russian intellectual. She spends two weeks visiting the mansion of author Hypo Wilson and his wife Alma, Miriam’s old schoolmate. While there she meets author Miss Prout, another friend of Hypo’s.

The Wilsons are generally understood to be proxies for H. G. Wells and Amy Catherine Robbins Wells. Miss Prout is thought to be based on Violet Hunt.

items.title: The Clever Woman of the Family
items.author: Charlotte M. Yonge
items.content: Unsatisfied with the rigid gender roles of her small seaside community, Rachel Curtis yearns to use her cleverness to find a purpose in life. Seeking to make the world a better place for women, she dives into intellectual battles, writes opinionated articles, and dreams of liberating oppressed women from lace-making and marriage. Acting as her foils are Lady Temple, a widow with an army of small children, and Miss Williams, a young woman left deformed and scarred by a horrible accident in her youth. As she strives to make her dreams come true, her small community will cause Rachel’s cleverness to be opposed, tried, and tested, making her carefully consider: is she truly the clever woman of the family?

items.title: Cogewea, the Half-Blood
items.author: Mourning Dove
items.content:
Cogewea, a mischievous young rancher, lives with her older sister and brother-in-law on their homestead, the Horseshoe Bend Ranch, located in the Flathead Indian Reservation. A member of the Okanogan tribe, Cogewea is nevertheless stigmatized as a “breed”—a derogatory term historically applied to people of mixed Native American and European descent. Drama arrives at the Horseshoe Bend with the person of Alfred Densmore, a businessman who has set out from the Eastern states in search of adventure and money. After he breaks his arm by being thrown by a half-tame bronco, Densmore develops a romantic interest in Cogewea, sparking a rivalry with Cogewea’s friend Jim, who is the ranch’s foreman and a fellow breed. Cogewea must navigate the interwoven challenges of choosing a suitor and reckoning with her ethnic identity, with the aid of advice in the form of stories told by her grandmother, the Stemteemä.

was one of the first novels ever published by a Native American woman. It was the product of collaboration between Mourning Dove and her editor, Lucullus Virgil McWhorter, a Euro-American anthropologist and advocate of indigenous American cultures. Critics have debated the extent of McWhorter’s influence on the final product, but Mourning Dove’s own correspondence with McWhorter suggests that McWhorter revised her draft significantly and introduced his own voice into the novel. continues to be studied as an early example of Native American literature.

items.title: The House of Rimmon
items.author: Henry van Dyke Jr.
items.content:
After being betrayed by his beloved wife, the commander of the Syrian army, Naaman, finds help from a captive maid, Ruahmah. Cursed with leprosy by his god, Naaman is led by Ruahmah to Elisha, a prophet of her people’s god. Along the way, Naaman is confronted by his own commitments to faith, honor, and his nation.

In this dramatic adaptation of the story of Naaman and Elisha, Henry van Dyke illuminates a brief but intriguing Biblical narrative, interweaving themes of love, patriotism, and fidelity.

items.title: The Beggar’s Opera
items.author: John Gay
items.content:
Peachum’s racket—running a gang of thieves who prey on London’s well-to-do—is paying great dividends, but what wasn’t in his plans was his daughter secretly marrying his most profitable rogue, the highwayman Captain Macheath. The best way out of the situation seems to be to collaborate with Lockit, the corrupt jailer of Newgate prison, to see Macheath hanged for his crimes—but it turns out that it’s not just Polly whom Macheath has been having a dalliance with.

was written as a satire of the fashionable Italian operas of the time, riffing on the same form but moving the setting from the upper-class sphere to something decidedly more down-to-earth. The music, similarly, was arranged from popular songs that the audience would have been familiar with. It was enormously popular, enjoying the then-longest theatrical run in London. A contemporary review, referring to the writer John Gay and director John Rich, quipped that “it has made Rich very Gay, and probably will make Gay very Rich.” But not all of the critics were quite so positive, with some criticizing the thinly veiled satire of then-prominent public figures.

The opera remained enduringly popular after its initial run, though the sequel was seen to be a step too far and was banned. had its biggest revival in the 1920s, inspiring Berthold Brecht’s and numerous other global performances and adaptations.

items.title: The Great Airport Mystery
items.author: Franklin W. Dixon
items.content:
It’s almost the end of term for the Hardy boys and their chums. With tests and college (or a career as detectives) looming, the boys decide to take a drive to a newly constructed airport. However, their sightseeing quickly turns sour as an airplane crashes, nearly killing them in the process. Sore over the witnesses and evidence taking the boys’ side, the guilty pilot seems bent on revenge. The question is: just how far will he go?

This book was published in 1930 and then rewritten in 1965. This Standard Ebooks edition follows the original 1930 edition.

items.title: The Home and the World
items.author: Rabindranath Tagore
items.content:
The wealthy Bengali zamindar Nikhil has spent his last nine years of marriage trying to modernize and westernize his wife Bimala. But when he invites his friend Sandip, a fiery pro-Swadeshi activist fighting for Indian independence, to his home, Bimala becomes enraptured by the nationalist cause—and by the fascinating figure himself.

is a complex exploration of the contradictions of the anti-British Swadeshi movement in the early 1900s. Rabindranath Tagore was himself active in the early days of the movement, but later became disillusioned, for reasons this novel examines in depth. The novel is also an examination of the traditional organization of wealthy Bengali households, in which women are kept separate from the outside world.

was adapted into a 1984 Golden Palm nominated film by Satyajit Ray.
